Tolerance may develop to the anxiolytic effects of benzodiazepines although this appears to be less likely than tolerance to the psychomotor effects. No one benzodiazepine appears more effective than the others in the treatment of anxiety disorders.3 However, adverse ef- fects and pharmacokinetic parameters may influence choice. Buspirone, an azaspirodecanedione, appears to have broadly similar efficacy to the benzodiazepines but a slow- er onset of action; it may cause less sedation and depend- ence. It is reported to lack euphoriant effect. Its efficacy is reduced in patients who have had previous extensive use of benzodiazepines.4,5 Increasingly, antidepressants are considered preferable to benzodiazepines for the treatment of generalised anxiety disorder;1,2,4,6-10 they are particularly appropriate when medium or long-term therapy is necessary or when depres- sion is also present. They may take several weeks to have an effect, so combined therapy with benzodiazepines may be required initially. Tricyclic antidepressants such as imi- pramine have a proven benefit in the treatment of general- ised anxiety disorder.2-4,6-8 More recently, SSRIs have been used as alternatives;3,11,12 paroxetine has been the most extensively studied.8 The noradrenaline and seroton- in reuptake inhibitor venlafaxine may also be used.1,8 These relatively newer drugs are safer in overdose and are associated with less severe adverse effects than the tricy- clics and in the UK NICE1 and others9 consider SSRIs to be the antidepressants of choice in generalised anxiety dis- order. Beta blockers may be useful for the control of the physical symptoms of anxiety.12 There is little evidence to support the efficacy of antihistamines such as hydroxyzine in anx- ious patients,2 and the use of antihistamines solely for their sedative effect in anxiety is not considered appropriate. Antipsychotics have been used by some in severe anxiety for their sedative effects; long-term use should be avoided because of the risk of tardive dyskinesia. In a few studies, antiepileptics such as pregabalin and tiagabine have been found to be effective for the treatment of generalised anx- iety disorder.13 Anxiety may be present with other disorders such as de- pression in mixed anxiety and depressive disorders, the management of which is discussed under Depression on p.373. 1.
